paras: The 1888 election violence in Union County, Arkansas, was a series of floggings, beatings and reported killings of Black men by armed Democrats around the state election of September 3, 1888, centered on El Dorado. Press Neal, Sandy Newton and Aaron Cobb were among the men named as whipped, while the dead went unnamed and estimates ran from one or two Black men to a rumored sixteen. Northern Republican papers held up the county as an example of how the Democrats had carried Arkansas.

Union County, with El Dorado as its seat, lay on Arkansas's southern border without a railroad or telegraph. In the governor's race the Democrat Eagle faced Norwood, the candidate of the Union Labor party and reformers, whom leading Black men in the county planned to support. The week before the election, the printing office of the Union Labor newspaper at El Dorado was wrecked.

Norwood and Eagle both spoke at El Dorado on Saturday, September 1, and the whipping of Black men began that night. Press Neal, who lived eight miles north of El Dorado, was severely whipped for saying he would vote as he pleased, and Sandy Newton and Aaron Cobb, of different townships, were also whipped. A Little Rock dispatch citing "responsible white citizens" said Democrats warned leading Black men that they would be whipped or killed if they voted, then flogged twenty-five men from nearly every precinct.

On Sunday, by the same account, the attackers went to a Black church, killed one man and wounded several. That night about forty Black men took refuge in a hall over the store of J. G. Smith, an El Dorado reformer, until the mob, through messengers including W. C. Langford and J. C. Wright, told Smith he would hang within five minutes unless he turned them out; the men were finally allowed to go home.

Before daylight on election day, militia guarded the roads into El Dorado and turned Black men back with threats of death; some who took by-ways were shot at, and others were beaten at their homes. The Little Rock dispatch put 100 armed white men at Eldorado that morning and said that before the polls opened they had killed one Black man and nearly whipped another to death. Jordan Gray was stripped, pounded with guns and prodded with bayonets, and a Black man was reported killed at Lisbon. In Champagnolle precinct, three masked men seized and destroyed the ballot box between lines of armed militia.

According to the Little Rock dispatch, white witnesses opposed to the violence were then made at gunpoint to promise not to prosecute. The Cooper letter said many Black men had left the county and more would go before the year was out. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

All of the reports ran in Northern papers drawing on Little Rock dispatches or on letters from Republican and Union Labor men; no Arkansas paper's account appears in the coverage. The New-York Tribune broke the story on September 13 under "A Vote or a Life in Arkansas" and "Sixteen Men Killed in Union County," calling it "premeditated murder of negroes at the polls." The next day the Wilmington Daily Republican printed a brief Little Rock dispatch as "The Race War in Arkansas."

On September 17 the Tribune published the Cooper letter, the only report naming Neal, Newton and Cobb, as "Political Outrages in Arkansas," and the Oskaloosa Herald later quoted it in an editorial attacking Iowa Democrats. The Indianapolis Journal printed R. B. Carl Lee's letter as "Bloody Fraud in Arkansas," and two Vermont papers reprinted a New York Mail and Express summary, one headed "A Reign of Terror Again Inaugurated among the Blacks."

Accounts of the dead, none of them named, disagreed: the Little Rock dispatch counted killings at the church, at El Dorado and at Lisbon and passed on a rumor of sixteen dead, which the Daily Republican gave as sixteen "negroes." The Mail and Express summary gave one killed and one mortally wounded; the Cooper letter reported no deaths. Carl Lee alone wrote that seven white Union Labor men were shot dead on Monday, and he dated the whippings to Sunday night.

reader.title: 1888 election violence in Union County, Arkansas
bases: Armed Democrats and militia flogged some twenty-five Black men across the county's precincts, attacked a Black church and drove Black voters from the polls with guns around the September 3 election (A1, A3, A4); this was county-wide election violence, not whitecapping.

Three separate sources (Little Rock informants in A1/A2, the letter to the Republican committee in A3/A6, Carl Lee's letter in A4) agree that armed Democrats whipped many Black men and drove Black voters from the polls; the number and race of those killed are contested (A1, A4, A5).

accounts.label: Little Rock dispatch from Union County white citizens
accounts.gist: Democrats flogged twenty-five Black men Saturday night, killed one at a church Sunday, and on election morning 100 armed white men at Eldorado killed one and nearly whipped another to death; sixteen were rumored killed.

accounts.label: Letter to the Republican State Central Committee
accounts.gist: Whipping of influential Black men such as Press Neal began the night of September 1; militia turned Black voters away from El Dorado on election day; a mob threatened to hang J. G. Smith for sheltering forty Black men.

accounts.label: Union Labor leader R. B. Carl Lee
accounts.gist: Democratic clubs armed with state rifles whipped over twenty Black men Sunday night and on Monday killed seven white Union Labor men and wounded over twenty.

framing.detail: New-York Tribune headlined 'A Vote or a Life in Arkansas' and 'Premeditated Murder of Negroes at the Polls'.
Wilmington Daily Republican ran the brief dispatch as 'The Race War in Arkansas' without comment.
Tribune called them 'outrages without parallel in the political history of the State'.
Indianapolis Journal: 'Bloody Fraud in Arkansas', a story 'so startling that it is almost incredible'.
Mail and Express summary, 'How Arkansas Was Carried', asks what Northern Democrats think of these methods.
Oskaloosa Herald used the report to attack local Democrats as apologists for 'horrible outrages'.

versions.value: One Black man killed at a church Sunday, one killed and one expected to die at El Dorado Monday, one killed at Lisbon; sixteen rumored
Sixteen Black men killed about election time, per one white man
One Black man killed and another mortally wounded at a church
Seven white Union Labor men killed Monday

conflicts.note: All killing figures are unnamed and secondhand; the A3/A6 letter, the most detailed local account, reports whippings, shooting at and beating but no deaths.
A1 and A3 independently give Saturday.

versions.value: Democratic clubs armed by Governor Hughes with state Winchesters and made into militia companies
